story.headline: The Federal Reserve held rates but two officials voted to hike, and chair Kevin Warsh's patient tone pulled the dollar off a two-week high. Canada raised rates; the UK Budget passed calmly.

reads.policy: The Fed held but two officials wanted to hike now, and Canada raised rates, so the global push toward higher rates continues. Fed chair Kevin Warsh refused to commit to December, which took some shine off the dollar. Europe and Japan decide next, and both are expected to wait until December.
reads.growth: The Fed upgraded its view of the US economy to strong, while Britain's budget watchdog cut its growth forecast and German shoppers stayed gloomy. That gap keeps favouring the dollar. US third-quarter growth figures on Thursday are the next check.
reads.inflation: Energy keeps pushing prices up: the Fed called inflation elevated, Canada raised its inflation forecasts and Australia's ran hotter than its central bank expected. That keeps most banks leaning toward hikes, which supports currencies whose banks act. The US inflation measure the Fed watches most comes on Thursday.
reads.risk: Markets stayed calm through the Fed, so the yen and franc drew little demand as safe places for money. The risks are building in the background: a report says the US may strike Iran after the midterms, and Israel's election left no clear winner. A turn in either would test that calm.
reads.tot: Oil rose again on falling US stocks and talk of US strikes on Iran after the midterms. That helps exporters like Canada and Australia and costs importers like Japan and the euro area. Until the talks with Iran produce terms, the war premium stays in the price.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, but Canada's rate hike today was too cautious to force them to buy loonies back. Their bets against the kiwi paid off after New Zealand's surprise hold. In the pound and the Aussie, hedge funds and long-term investors take opposite sides.
reads.fiscal: Chancellor John Healey's first UK Budget passed calmly, with borrowing set to fall, so UK bonds and the pound took it in stride. France's budget fight is still unresolved and keeps a weight on the euro.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28, but two officials voted to hike, and markets see a December hike as very likely. Chair Kevin Warsh refused to commit to a date, which took some lift off the dollar.
fed.why: Energy-driven inflation is still well above the Fed's goal and the economy is growing strongly, but Warsh points to tighter credit and calmer inflation expectations as reasons for patience.
fed.watch: US growth and PCE inflation figures at 7:30 AM CT Thursday, then the December 9 decision, which brings new forecasts. Hot inflation would make December look settled.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% on October 28, its first hike since 2023, and said more may be needed. It plans to move carefully, so the loonie got little lift.
boc.priced: December: another hike possible, about a coin toss.
boc.why: Energy and import costs have pushed Canadian inflation above the bank's range, and it now expects inflation to stay high through next year, even as US tariffs keep the economy soft.
boc.watch: Comments from deputy governor Nicolas Vincent on Thursday, Canada's GDP on Friday and the December 9 decision.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised markets by holding at 2.75% instead of hiking, which knocked the kiwi down. All members still expect more tightening, so December is open.
rbnz.priced: December: a hike possible; no firm odds yet.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the bank's target band, but a narrow majority wanted to see how this year's hikes are working before going further.
rbnz.watch: Comments from Governor Anna Breman and the December 9 decision, which comes with a full policy statement and new forecasts.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank is expected to hold on Thursday and raise rates in December, because energy keeps euro-area inflation high. France's debt troubles limit how much that helps the euro.
ecb.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
ecb.why: Energy costs keep inflation well above the bank's 2% goal, while growth is slowing and France's budget fight adds risk.
ecb.watch: Euro-area economic sentiment early Thursday, then the decision at 8:15 AM CT and President Christine Lagarde's press conference at about 8:45 AM CT, especially anything on French bonds or a December hike.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan is expected to hold on Friday and raise rates in December. Underlying inflation in Japan is now at a three-year high, but rates are still far below other major economies', which keeps the yen weak.
boj.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
boj.why: Inflation is broadening beyond energy, with the bank's own underlying gauge at a three-year high, which builds the case for a hike.
boj.watch: Tokyo consumer prices at 6:30 PM CT tonight, then the decision and new forecasts on Friday, Japan time (Thursday night CT). Any move by Tokyo to buy yen would also matter.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia is now expected to raise rates on November 3, after inflation came in above its own forecast. That supports the Aussie.
rba.why: Underlying prices are rising faster than the bank forecast in August, partly because of fuel costs, and Governor Michele Bullock says the board will debate whether this year's four hikes are enough.
rba.watch: The decision at 9:30 PM CT Monday, November 2, with new forecasts; a weak jobs market is the main reason the bank could still wait.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is all but certain to raise rates on November 5 because UK inflation is running hot. That supports the pound, and Chancellor John Healey's calm first Budget removed a near-term risk.
boe.priced: November: hike all but certain; December: a second hike possible.
boe.why: UK inflation is well above target, and shop prices are now rising at their fastest pace in two and a half years as energy costs spread.
boe.watch: The November 5 decision at 6:00 AM CT, and whether the bank signals a second hike in December. Slower growth forecasts in the Budget could make it cautious.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds rates at zero because Swiss inflation is near zero, and markets are split on its next step. That leaves the franc relying on its role as a safe place for money.
snb.priced: December: markets split; no move is the slight favourite.
snb.why: Inflation is near zero, so the bank has no reason to hike, and it has grown more relaxed about a weaker franc.
snb.watch: Comments from board member Petra Tschudin on Thursday and the December 10 decision; any remark on the franc matters most.

USD.summary: The dollar sits near the top of the board because US rates are among the highest of the majors and a December Federal Reserve hike looks very likely. It slipped after the Fed held rates and chair Kevin Warsh refused to commit to a date.

notes.policy: Two Fed officials voted to hike now and a December hike is mostly priced, which supports the dollar.
notes.inflation: High oil keeps US inflation well above the Fed's goal, which keeps pressure on it to raise rates.

EUR.summary: The euro is held back by weak euro-area growth, France's debt troubles and heavy energy costs, though an expected European Central Bank hike in December helps. It rose today only because the dollar slipped after the Fed.

notes.policy: The ECB is expected to hold on Thursday, so its December hike offers less near-term lift than rivals' moves.
notes.growth: Euro-area business surveys missed in October and German and French shoppers are gloomy.
notes.inflation: Energy keeps euro-area inflation high, which keeps a December ECB hike on the table.
notes.tot: The euro area imports most of its energy, so high oil drains money out of the region.
notes.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could force them to buy it back.
notes.fiscal: France's budget fight and heavy debt keep investors wary of French bonds and the euro.

GBP.summary: The pound is supported by an all but certain Bank of England hike on November 5 as UK inflation runs hot. Chancellor John Healey's first Budget passed calmly, removing a near-term risk.

notes.policy: A Bank of England hike on November 5 is nearly fully expected, the firmest outlook among the major banks.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been strong, though the Budget watchdog cut its growth forecast for next year.
notes.inflation: UK inflation is well above target and shop prices are rising faster, which keeps the bank on track to hike.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low because Japan's rates are far below other major economies' and the country imports costly energy. A Bank of Japan hike in December and Tokyo's warnings about stepping in are its main supports.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan is expected to hold this week, so the wide rate gap with the US still weighs on the yen.
notes.risk: The yen's role as a safe place for money gives it support whenever markets get nervous.
notes.tot: Japan imports almost all its energy, so high oil drains money out of the country and weakens the yen.

CHF.summary: The franc is held back by near-zero Swiss inflation and rates at zero, and leans on its role as a safe place for money. In calm markets that support is modest.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is near zero, so the Swiss National Bank has no reason to raise rates.
notes.risk: The franc's role as a safe place for money gives it support whenever markets get nervous.

AUD.summary: The Aussie is supported by a likely Reserve Bank of Australia hike on November 3 after inflation beat the bank's forecast, and it rose to a five-week high. A weak jobs market is the main thing holding it back.

notes.policy: A fifth rate hike this year on November 3 now looks likely, which supports the Aussie.
notes.growth: Australia's business surveys have slipped and unemployment is at a five-year high.
notes.inflation: Underlying prices rose faster than the bank expected last quarter, keeping pressure on it to hike.
notes.tot: Australia exports energy, so high prices bring money into the country.

CAD.summary: The loonie is supported by the Bank of Canada's first rate hike since 2023 and by high oil prices, while US tariffs weigh on Canada's economy. The bank's careful tone kept the hike from lifting it much.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates and left the door open to more, which supports the loonie.
notes.growth: Canada's economy is soft, with shoppers spending only modestly under US tariffs.
notes.inflation: Producer and import prices are rising fast, and the bank now expects inflation to stay high next year.
notes.tot: High oil prices bring more money into Canada, the biggest energy exporter among the majors.

NZD.summary: The kiwi fell after New Zealand's central bank held rates when markets expected a hike. The bank still expects to tighten later, and a steady economy and firm export prices limit the damage.

notes.growth: New Zealand's services sector keeps growing, a sign the economy is holding up.
notes.risk: The kiwi tends to do well when markets are calm, as they were through the Fed.
notes.tot: Firm dairy prices, New Zealand's biggest export, bring money into the country.
